result: Chick DRG axons exhibit strain-softening behavior where the steady-state elastic modulus decreases with increasing strain, accompanied by tension homeostasis where tension relaxes to similar steady-state values across strain steps. This viscoelastic solid-like response is reversible, with axons recovering their initial length within 5-10 seconds after release.
evaluation: Claims C2, C17-C20, C22-C24 collectively demonstrate strain-softening through direct mechanical measurements (Figure 2B-D), showing force relaxation after strain steps (C17), tension saturation with increasing strain (C18, C22), solid-like behavior at longer timescales (C19, C20), and reversibility (C23, C24). The experimental data with multiple axons and repeated measurements on the same axons provide strong converging evidence.

result: F-actin plays a more significant mechanical role than microtubules in axonal stretch response. Latrunculin-A treatment produces a more dramatic reduction in steady-state tension and faster relaxation compared to Nocodazole treatment, while both Taxol and Jasplakinolide preserve strain-softening with Jasplakinolide causing larger increases in moduli.
evaluation: Claims C25-C30, C32 are supported by systematic pharmacological perturbation experiments (Figure 3). The comparison shows F-actin disruption (Lat-A) causes greater tension reduction (C29: 13.0→1.8 nN) than microtubule disruption (Noco: 9.3→5.8 nN) (C28), with faster relaxation (C30). The Taxol pre-treatment control (C32) rules out secondary microtubule effects. Blebbistatin controls (C27) exclude myosin-II involvement.

result: The periodic actin-spectrin lattice is present in all axons, becomes more prevalent with culture age while maintaining ~190-200 nm periodicity, and contributes prominently to axonal mechanics. β-II spectrin knockdown dramatically reduces steady-state tension, correlating with reduced spectrin content.
evaluation: Claims C33-C38, C40-C41 are supported by complementary imaging (confocal, STED) and mechanical measurements. STED shows periodic structure in all axons (C33, n=180), increasing prevalence with age (C34, Appendix 1-table 1), preservation after Taxol/Jasplakinolide (C35) but loss after Lat-A (C37). Correlation between lattice prevalence and mechanical stiffness (C38, Figure 4B) and morpholino knockdown effects (C40-C41, Figure 4C) provide strong functional evidence.

result: A theoretical model based on force-dependent unfolding/refolding of spectrin repeats can explain the observed strain-softening and predicts non-monotonic relaxation time dependence on strain. The estimated spectrin contribution (6-10 nN) is comparable to measured axon tension in 4-DIV axons.
evaluation: Claims C4, C42-C43, C45, C47-C49 present a coherent theoretical framework supported by prior AFM data (C42, Rief et al. 1999) and geometric estimates (C47-C48). The model qualitatively reproduces experimental observations including strain-softening (Figure 5B) and non-monotonic relaxation time (C45, Figure 5C-D). The order-of-magnitude estimate (C48-C49) provides plausibility but requires more rigorous validation.

result: Axons experience significant stretch deformations in vivo during normal activities and impacts, with strains ranging from 2-5% in the brain during jumping to 30% in sciatic nerves during limb movements, and up to 160% in specialized whale nerves.
evaluation: Claims C1, C9-C13 establish the physiological context through citations to peer-reviewed studies. The cited values are specific and verifiable (Phillips et al. 2004 for 30% strain, Bayly et al. 2005 for 2-5% brain strain, etc.). Claims C6-C8 describe established axonal ultrastructure supported by citations and Figure 1.

result: Prior work has established that axons respond viscoelastically to stretch and can develop excess tension through myosin-II molecular motor activity.
evaluation: Claims C14-C16 accurately summarize prior literature (Dennerll et al. 1989, Bernal et al. 2007, O'Toole et al. 2015, etc.). These are background claims supported by appropriate citations that contextualize the current work.

result: Chick DRG axons used in this study are approximately 1 μm in diameter with actin-spectrin rings spaced ~190-200 nm apart, corresponding to the α/β spectrin tetramer length.
evaluation: Claims C21 and C63 describe the experimental system characteristics supported by direct measurements and autocorrelation analysis (Figure 4B inset). The periodicity matches prior literature (Xu et al. 2013, D'Este et al. 2015) and is consistently observed across multiple DIV conditions (Appendix 1-table 1, Figure 4-figure supplement 3).

result: Prior studies in C. elegans and red blood cells support the mechanical importance of spectrin, showing that spectrin knockouts cause axon breakage, spectrin is under pre-stress, and spectrin-mediated softening occurs in RBCs through domain unfolding.
evaluation: Claims C50-C53 accurately cite relevant prior work (Hammarlund et al. 2007, Krieg et al. 2014, Lee and Discher 2001, Johnson et al. 2007, etc.) that provides supporting context for the spectrin mechanism proposed in this study. The citations are appropriate and accurately represented.

result: The axonal strain-softening response contrasts with strain-stiffening observed in many other cell types, which arises from entropic F-actin behavior and can transition to softening at higher strains through cross-link detachment or filament buckling.
evaluation: Claims C54-C57 accurately contrast the current findings with established cell mechanics literature (Fernández et al. 2006, Storm et al. 2005, Gardel et al. 2004, Trepat et al. 2007-2008). The distinctions drawn are appropriate and help contextualize the novelty of the axonal response.

result: Spectrin mutations are associated with neurological disorders including spinocerebellar ataxia and early infantile epileptic encephalopathies.
evaluation: Claims C58-C59 cite appropriate medical literature (Ikeda et al. 2006, Wang et al. 2018) establishing clinical relevance. These are factual statements about disease associations that provide medical context for the findings.

result: The experimental methods include primary chick DRG neuron culture, morpholino transfection validated by fluorescence, force apparatus validation using cantilever controls, and experiments performed at room temperature to suppress active dynamics.
evaluation: Claims C60-C62, C64-C65 describe methodological details supported by the Materials and Methods section. Transfection efficiency (C62, n=46 showing fluorescence), apparatus validation (C64), and temperature control (C65, with citations Yengo et al. 2012, Hong et al. 2016) are appropriately documented.
